body:
## Module 1 in two minutes

**Fluency isn't practice.** 101 taught you to use AI well; nothing about using it well makes it repeatable. Everything you do with AI is still handmade — context retyped, quality varying with your energy, nothing a colleague could run. The Practitioner's jump is from tasks to systems.

**Every repeatable workflow has five parts:** trigger, inputs, transformation, verification, output-with-owner. Your recurring tasks already have these parts implicitly; drawing them out exposes which one is missing. It's almost always verification.

**Audit, don't remember.** Memory nominates the loudest task; last week's calendar and sent mail nominate the true candidates. A candidate must recur, have a shape, and run on material you supply.

**Your first build: high frequency, high structure, owned inputs, low stakes.** Not the most annoying task (annoyance often means the task resists structure) and not the highest-stakes one (you'll make your learning mistakes on it). Boring is a feature — the impressive build comes second, and inherits working habits.

### The practitioner's heuristic

You may only systematize what you have verified by hand. And a workflow, like a model, must not make decisions about people — automation makes decisions faster, not fairer.

**The full module adds** the audit method, the selection rules with their two seductive wrong answers, a twelve-task sorting exercise from a People leader's real week, and the capstone's first stage: choosing your build and writing its five-part spec — the artifact all seven later modules advance.
